lesson.title: The Sharp Point: Cusps
lesson.summary: A cusp is a point where a function is continuous but its one-sided derivatives both diverge to infinity with opposite signs, producing a sharply pointed graph rather than a smooth curve or a plain corner.
lesson.body:
A cusp is a second way that differentiability can fail at a point where the function is still continuous, but it looks quite different from a corner. At a corner, both one-sided derivatives exist as finite numbers that simply disagree. At a cusp, neither one-sided derivative is finite at all: the difference quotient grows without bound as h shrinks to 0, and critically, it grows toward positive infinity on one side and toward negative infinity on the other. The tangent line becomes vertical from both directions, but the curve approaches that vertical line from opposite rotational senses, producing a sharp point that looks like the tip of a beak rather than a bent line.

Consider f(x) = the square root of the absolute value of x, evaluated near a = 0. For x > 0, this is simply the square root of x, with derivative 1 / (2 times the square root of x). As x approaches 0 from the right, the square root of x shrinks toward 0, so this derivative grows without bound toward positive infinity, meaning f'_+(0) = positive infinity. For x < 0, the function is the square root of -x, and by the chain rule its derivative is -1 / (2 times the square root of -x). As x approaches 0 from the left, the square root of -x also shrinks toward 0, but the leading minus sign sends the whole expression toward negative infinity, so f'_-(0) = negative infinity.

The two one-sided derivatives diverge to opposite infinities, which is exactly the signature of a cusp. Geometrically, the graph plunges down steeply from the left, becoming momentarily vertical right at the origin, then shoots back up just as steeply on the right, all while staying continuous and touching the single point (0, 0) at the bottom. There is no way to draw a single straight tangent line through that point, because the curve is effectively doubling back on itself in slope, even though it never doubles back in value.

It helps to contrast a cusp with the corner point from the previous section and with the vertical tangent point discussed next. A corner has finite slopes on both sides that disagree. A cusp has infinite slopes on both sides that point in genuinely opposite directions, positive infinity versus negative infinity. A vertical tangent point, by contrast, also has infinite slopes on both sides, but with the same sign, so the curve passes straight through rather than turning back. All three share the property that f is continuous at the point but the derivative limit does not exist as a finite number, which is exactly why they all belong to the broader family of non-differentiable points.

Cusps are not just curiosities invented for homework. Many physical boundaries, such as the outline of a raindrop as it falls and flattens, or the envelope curve traced by a family of light rays in an optical caustic, have genuine cusp points where the boundary comes to a sharp, momentarily vertical point. Recognizing the algebraic signature, opposite-signed infinite one-sided derivatives, lets you identify a cusp directly from a formula without needing to see the picture first.
